questions.title: Describe an RTOS
questions.text: Describe a **real-time operating system**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Processes inputs / responds within a guaranteed time / deadline (1)
- to monitor and control a physical process as it happens, e.g. airbag, robot (1)
scheme.model_answer: An OS that responds to inputs within a guaranteed deadline so it can control a physical system as events happen, such as an airbag.

questions.title: RTOS features
questions.text: Select **two** features of a real-time operating system.

options.content: Central user accounts for a whole network

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Deterministic
questions.text: Explain why an RTOS must be **deterministic**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Its response time must be predictable / always within the deadline (1)
- otherwise the controlled system could fail / be dangerous, e.g. brakes respond late (1)
scheme.model_answer: The time it takes to respond must always be predictable and within the deadline; if it varied, an airbag or brake system could respond too late and cause injury.

questions.title: Priority scheduling
questions.text: In a greenhouse RTOS, the fire sensor triggers while the system is updating the humidity display. Explain what the RTOS does.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The fire task has a higher priority, so it pre-empts / interrupts the display task (1)
- the alarm / heater switch-off runs immediately; the display task continues later (1)
scheme.model_answer: The fire task has the highest priority, so the RTOS immediately interrupts the display update, sounds the alarm and switches off the heaters, then returns to the display task.

questions.title: Hard or soft
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each system is hard or soft real-time.

scheme.mark_scheme: Flight control hard (1); video call soft (1); robot hard (1); game soft (1)

questions.title: RTOS vs general-purpose OS
questions.text: Give **two** differences between a real-time OS and a general-purpose OS such as Windows.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides: guaranteed deadlines vs good average speed; strict priority vs time-sharing / fairness; deterministic vs variable response; small embedded vs large; minimal vs rich interface
scheme.model_answer: 1 An RTOS guarantees a response within a deadline, whereas Windows aims for good average speed. 2 An RTOS is small and embedded with little interface, whereas Windows has a rich GUI.

questions.title: Describe a NOS
questions.text: Describe a **network operating system**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- An OS that manages a network and its shared resources (files, printers, applications) (1)
- and its users / accounts / security, usually running on a server (1)
scheme.model_answer: An OS, usually on a server, that manages the users of a network and the resources they share, such as files and printers.

questions.title: User account management
questions.text: Describe how a network operating system implements user account management.

scheme.mark_scheme: NOS provides user authentication and authorization mechanisms… (1) … ensuring that only authorized users can access network resources. (1) NOS verifies user identities… (1) … to assign appropriate access rights. (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: The NOS verifies each user's identity at log-in and then gives them the access rights of their account and groups, so only authorised users can use each resource.

questions.title: NOS functions
questions.text: Match each NOS function to its description.

right.text: Checks the user name and password at log-in
Decides which folders a user may open
Orders documents waiting for a shared printer
Records who accessed which file and when

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Client–server vs peer-to-peer
questions.text: Give **two** differences between a client–server network managed by a NOS and a peer-to-peer network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): centralised vs each computer manages itself; strong central security vs weaker; central backup vs individual; needs server / admin vs cheap; large vs small networks
scheme.model_answer: 1 Client–server has central control of accounts and security on the server, whereas in peer-to-peer each computer manages itself. 2 Client–server backs up data centrally, whereas peer-to-peer users back up their own files.

questions.title: Central backup
questions.text: A network operating system can back up all users' files centrally on the server.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Batch features
questions.text: Some computers use batch operating systems. Give **two** features of the batch operating system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Jobs with similar requirements are batched together and run through the computer as a group (1); data is collected for a defined period of time and processed as a pack of similar tasks (1); sorting is performed before processing (1); no user interaction (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: 1 Jobs with similar requirements are grouped and run together. 2 Data is collected over a period and processed without user interaction.

questions.title: Batch steps
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Batch jobs wait in a job [[1]]. The input data is often [[2]] before processing. The output for slow printers is placed in a queue — this is called [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) queue (2) sorted (3) spooling

questions.title: Why batch
questions.text: Explain why batch processing is used to produce 300 000 water bills every quarter.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): large number of similar jobs; readings collected over the quarter and processed together; not needed immediately; runs automatically at night / off-peak without operator
scheme.model_answer: All 300 000 bills are similar calculations made only once a quarter, so the meter readings can be collected and processed together automatically overnight.

questions.title: Batch disadvantage
questions.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of batch processing.

scheme.mark_scheme: Disadvantage (1) + explanation (1): delay — results not immediate / data out of date; errors found only after the batch runs — whole batch repeated; no interaction — jobs cannot be changed
scheme.model_answer: Results are not immediate: a customer's payment made today only appears after the overnight batch has run.

questions.title: Choose the OS type
questions.text: Tick (✓) the most suitable OS type for each scenario.

prefill: Overnight processing of all card payments at a bank
An office of 200 staff sharing folders and printers
Traffic lights that react to sensors at a junction

scheme.mark_scheme: Card payments batch (1); pacemaker real-time (1); office network (1); traffic lights real-time (1)

questions.title: Compare the three OS types
questions.text: A hospital uses a real-time OS in its patient monitors, a network OS on its servers and a batch OS for its monthly billing. Describe and compare these three types of operating system, explaining why each suits its use.

scheme.mark_scheme:
RTOS (max 2): guaranteed deadline / deterministic / priority; suits monitors because alarms must be immediate
NOS (max 2): manages users, access rights, shared records; suits servers because many staff share data securely
Batch (max 2): groups similar jobs, no interaction, scheduled; suits monthly bills — large volume, not urgent
Comparison points credited within each
scheme.model_answer: The real-time OS responds to sensor readings within a guaranteed deadline and gives the alarm task the highest priority, which suits patient monitors because a dangerous heart rate must trigger an alarm immediately. The network OS manages user accounts, authentication and access rights to shared files on the servers, so hundreds of staff can securely open the patient records they are allowed to see. The batch OS groups the month's treatments and runs the billing jobs automatically overnight without interaction, which suits billing because there are many similar bills and they are not urgent. Unlike the RTOS, the batch OS does not respond immediately, and unlike the NOS it has no interactive users while running.

questions.title: A greenhouse controller
questions.text: An agricultural company uses a real-time operating system to control the temperature, humidity and fire safety of its greenhouses.

scheme.mark_scheme: Guaranteed response / deadline (1); controls a process as it happens (1)
scheme.model_answer: An OS that responds to sensor inputs within a guaranteed time so it can control the greenhouse as conditions change.

parts.title: Features
parts.text: State **two** features of the RTOS, other than its response time.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): priority pre-emptive scheduling; deterministic; continuous monitoring / feedback; reliable / fault tolerant; small embedded; minimal interface; fast interrupt handling
scheme.model_answer: 1 Priority-based scheduling. 2 Continuous monitoring of sensors with feedback.

parts.title: Priority
parts.text: The fire sensor triggers while the RTOS is logging humidity data. Explain what happens.

scheme.mark_scheme: Fire task higher priority pre-empts logging (1); alarm / sprinklers / heaters off immediately, logging resumes after (1)
scheme.model_answer: The fire task has a higher priority, so it interrupts the logging task at once and switches on the alarm and sprinklers; the logging continues afterwards.

parts.title: Hard or soft
parts.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each system is hard or soft real-time.

prefill: Live video stream from a greenhouse camera

scheme.mark_scheme: Fire-safety hard (1); video soft (1); ABS hard (1)

parts.title: Embedded
parts.text: State **one** other device that uses an embedded real-time OS.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): airbag controller; pacemaker; autopilot; industrial robot; traffic lights; washing machine controller; drone
scheme.model_answer: A car airbag controller.

questions.title: A school network
questions.text: A school has 400 computers connected to servers that run a network operating system.

parts.title: User accounts
parts.text: Describe how a network operating system implements user account management.

scheme.mark_scheme: NOS provides user authentication and authorization mechanisms… (1) ensuring only authorized users access network resources (1); verifies identities (1) to assign access rights (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: It verifies each user's name and password at log-in and gives the account the access rights of its group, so only authorised users can use each resource.

parts.title: Other functions
parts.text: State **two** other functions of the NOS.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): file sharing; printer sharing / queues; central backup; security / logs; updates; remote administration; DHCP / DNS / e-mail
scheme.model_answer: 1 Sharing printers. 2 Backing up users' files centrally.

parts.title: Client–server
parts.text: Compare the school's client–server network with a peer-to-peer network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides: central vs individual control; security; backup; cost; size
scheme.model_answer: In the school's network the server controls all accounts and backups centrally, whereas in peer-to-peer each computer manages its own security and files, which would be impossible to control for 400 computers.

parts.title: Authentication vs authorisation
parts.text: Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Authentication — verifying who the user is (1); authorisation — deciding what the user may access (1)
scheme.model_answer: Authentication checks who the user is, for example by password; authorisation then decides which folders and printers that user may use.

parts.title: Central backup
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of the NOS backing up pupils' work centrally.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage (1) + explanation (1): automatic / regular — pupils do not need to remember; work can be restored if a PC fails / file deleted
scheme.model_answer: Backups happen automatically every night, so pupils' work can be restored even if they forget to save a copy or a computer fails.

questions.title: A water company
questions.text: A water company produces bills for 300 000 customers every quarter using a batch processing operating system.

parts.title: Features
parts.text: Give **two** features of the batch operating system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Jobs with similar requirements are batched together and run as a group (1); data collected for a defined period and processed as a pack (1); sorting before processing (1); no interaction (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: 1 Similar jobs are grouped and run together. 2 Data is collected over a period and processed without user interaction.

parts.title: How it works
parts.text: Describe how the billing jobs are processed by the batch OS.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): jobs submitted with instructions in advance (JCL / script); placed in a job queue; data sorted (by customer number); run automatically one after another at a scheduled / off-peak time; output spooled to printers / files
scheme.model_answer: The billing jobs are submitted with instructions written in advance and placed in a job queue. The meter readings are sorted by customer number, and at night the OS runs the jobs one after another without an operator, spooling the bills to the printers.

parts.title: Suitability
parts.text: Explain why batch processing is suitable for producing the bills.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): large volume of similar jobs; not urgent / quarterly; readings collected over the period; off-peak automatic
scheme.model_answer: There are 300 000 similar bills that are only needed once a quarter, so they can all be calculated together automatically at night.

parts.title: Disadvantage
parts.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of batch processing for the company.

scheme.mark_scheme: Disadvantage (1) + explanation (1): error found after the whole batch — all bills reprinted; results delayed; cannot change jobs while running
scheme.model_answer: If there is an error in the tariff, it may only be noticed after all 300 000 bills are printed, and the whole batch must be run again.

parts.title: When
parts.text: State when batch jobs are usually run and why.

scheme.mark_scheme: At night / off-peak, when the computer is not busy with other work (1)
scheme.model_answer: At night, when the computer is not needed for other work.

summary: Real-time, network and batch processing operating systems in depth — how each works, their key features, scheduling and interrupts in real-time systems, client–server and peer-to-peer networks and user account management in a NOS, job queues and scheduling in batch systems, and how to choose the right type.

blocks.content: Operating systems are designed for different **workloads**. A laptop OS is optimised for **one user running many programs**; other systems must react **instantly**, serve **hundreds of users over a network**, or process **millions of records without anyone watching**.

blocks.title: Three specialised OS types
rows: **Process large volumes of similar jobs efficiently**
Little or none; sensors and actuators
Many users at once over the network
Servers in schools, offices, data centres
Windows Server, Linux server, Novell NetWare
IBM z/OS (JCL jobs), scheduled jobs on servers

blocks.content: An operating system that **processes data and responds to events within a strict, guaranteed time limit (deadline)**, so that it can **monitor and control** a physical process as it happens. Correctness depends not only on the **result** but also on **when** it is produced.

items.title: Key features
items.content:
- **Deterministic** — the time to respond to an event is **predictable** and always within the deadline.
- **Priority-based pre-emptive scheduling** — the most urgent task **interrupts** lower-priority tasks immediately.
- **Fast interrupt handling** — very low **interrupt latency** (the time from a signal to the start of its handler).
- **Continuous monitoring** of sensors with **feedback** to control actuators (motors, valves, displays).
- **High reliability and fault tolerance** — runs for years without restarting; often has redundant components.
- **Small and efficient** — stored in ROM / flash in an **embedded** device; minimal or no user interface.

items.title: Hard vs soft real-time
items.content:
- **Hard** real-time: missing a deadline is a **failure** that may be dangerous — airbags, anti-lock brakes, pacemakers, aircraft flight control, industrial robots.
- **Soft** real-time: missing a deadline only **reduces quality** — video streaming, online games, VoIP calls, ticket booking.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  S[Sensor measures a value, e.g. temperature] --> I[Interrupt or regular sampling]
  I --> P[RTOS runs the highest-priority task within the deadline]
  P --> D{Value outside the limits?}
  D -- Yes --> A[Actuator acts, e.g. turns heater off]
  D -- No --> W[Wait for next reading]
  A --> S
  W --> S

blocks.title: A greenhouse control system
blocks.content: Sensors measure **temperature** and **humidity** every second. If the temperature rises above 30 °C, the RTOS must open the windows **within 2 seconds**; if a fire sensor triggers, the **highest-priority** task sounds the alarm and switches off the heaters **immediately**, interrupting any other task.

An operating system that **manages a network** of computers and its **shared resources** — files, printers, applications, Internet access — and the **users** who access them. It usually runs on a **server**, and client computers connect to it.

blocks.title: Client–server and peer-to-peer networks
rows: **Centralised** — the server manages accounts, security and backups
Strong; one place to set access rights
Each user backs up their own files

items.title: Functions of a NOS
items.content:
- **User account management** — creates accounts and **groups**, sets **passwords** and **password policies**.
- **Authentication and authorisation** — verifies who the user is and gives **access rights** to resources.
- **File and printer sharing** — central storage, home folders, print queues.
- **Security** — firewall, encryption, **audit logs** of who accessed what.
- **Centralised backup** and **software updates** for all clients.
- **Remote administration** and **network services** — DHCP, DNS, e-mail, web.
- Supports **many users simultaneously**.

items.title: How user account management works
items.content:
1. The administrator creates an **account** for each user and adds it to **groups** (e.g. Teachers, Grade 11).
2. When a user **logs in**, the NOS **verifies their identity** (user name + password / 2FA) — **authentication**.
3. The NOS checks the **access rights** of the user's account and groups — **authorisation**.
4. The user can only open the folders and printers they are allowed to use; every access may be **logged**.

blocks.title: Access rights on a school server
blocks.content:
| Folder | Teachers | Grade 11 pupils | Office staff |
|---|---|---|---|
| \\Exams | Read / write | No access | No access |
| \\Homework\\Grade11 | Read / write | Read | No access |
| \\Finance | No access | No access | Read / write |

An operating system that **groups jobs with similar requirements into batches** and **runs them one after another automatically**, **without user interaction**, usually at a **scheduled time**. Data is **collected over a period** and processed together.

blocks.title: How batch processing works
items: Jobs (programs + their data) are **submitted** with instructions written in advance (e.g. a **job control language**, JCL, or a script).
Jobs are placed in a **job queue** and **grouped** with similar jobs.
Input data is often **sorted** first (e.g. by account number) so it matches the master file.
At the scheduled time (often **at night**), the OS runs the jobs **one by one**, without an operator.
Output (bills, payslips, reports) is **spooled** to printers or files.

items.title: Features
items.content:
- Jobs with similar requirements are **batched together** and run as a group.
- Data is **collected over a defined period** and processed as a pack.
- **No interaction** with users while the jobs run.
- **Sorting** before processing; **scheduling** at off-peak times.
- **Spooling** — output is queued for slow devices such as printers.

items.title: Uses
items.content:
- **Payroll** at the end of each month.
- **Utility bills** and **bank statements**.
- End-of-day processing of **card transactions** and **cheques**.
- **Exam results**, census data, overnight database backups and reports.

blocks.title: Batch processing — advantages and disadvantages
rows: **Efficient** for very large volumes of similar data
Errors may be found only **after** the whole batch has run
Jobs cannot be changed while running
Not suitable for interactive or urgent tasks

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Give two features of the batch operating system. [2]**
Jobs with similar requirements are **batched together** and run through the computer **as a group** (1). Data is **collected for a defined period** of time and processed as a pack of similar tasks / **no user interaction** / sorting is performed before processing (1).

**Q: Describe how a network operating system implements user account management. [2]**
The NOS provides **authentication and authorisation** mechanisms, ensuring that **only authorised users can access network resources** (1); it **verifies user identities** to **assign appropriate access rights** (1).

**Q: Describe a real-time operating system. [2]**
It processes inputs and responds **within a guaranteed time / deadline** (1), so it can **control a physical process** as it happens, e.g. an airbag or a factory robot (1).

- Saying an RTOS is just "fast" — the key idea is a **guaranteed deadline** (predictability).
- Describing a NOS only as "an OS for the Internet" — it **manages users and shared resources** on a network.
- Saying batch processing lets users interact with jobs — it runs **without** interaction.
- Confusing **multi-user** (many users) with **network** OS (manages a network's resources) — a NOS is usually multi-user, but the focus is the network.
